name: Humburi Senni
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Heath, Jeffrey. 2014. Grammar of Humburi Senni (Songhay of Hombori, Mali). May 2014 version. Language Description Heritage Library, Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, Leipzig; University of Michigan Deep Blue, hdl 2027.42/117647. 449 pp.
catalog_locator: §3.9.1 'Lexical tones of syllables and stems', p. 51; §5.9.4 'Locative gà:', p. 258, directly below paradigm (300); §3.9.5.8 'Final-L Delinking', p. 100. The quote gives the p. 51 passage, then the p. 258 passage, then the p. 100 sentence, in that order.
catalog_quote: The basic stem-level melodies, which can be realized on stems or words of variable syllable count, are {H}, {L}, {HL}, and {LHL}. The only syllable-level tones are H, L, and <HL> (i.e. falling). Each of these occurs in both light and heavy word-final syllables, as shown in (29). ... In nonfinal syllables, only H and L occur, since tone breaks in {HL} and {LHL} melodies are bunched at the right edge of the word. ... Strikingly, <LH> (i.e. rising) tone is absent. ... Because of their prosodic heaviness, gà:-y-ndì and gà:-n-dòŋ in particular have some phonetic stress on their first syllables that can sound like H-tones. However, in my current interpretation they have the same (low) tones as in bà:-y-ndì+H ‘our share’, rather than the H-tone of má:y-ndì+H ‘our name’. ... However, in texts it is difficult to distinguish L- from H-tones in the first syllables of gà:-y-ndì and má:y-ndì+H, for example. Further study is needed. ... kûl ‘all’ is nearly always rhetorically “stressed.” The pitch of the preceding word is lowered to frame the high-pitched quantifier.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Humburi Senni is a tone language (syllable tones H, L, falling <HL>; stem melodies {H}, {L}, {HL}, {LHL}; no rising tone). The grammar's 449 pages contain no stress or accent section and state no word-stress rule; the only mention of stress is an incidental note that two prosodically heavy locative pronominals carry phonetic stress on their first syllable that can be mistaken for H-tone, plus 'rhetorical stress' (intonational emphasis) on kûl 'all'.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress system described). Phonetic first-syllable stress noted only for gà:-y-ndì, gà:-n-dòŋ (p. 258).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tonology; the stress remark concerns word-internal phonetic prominence in two inflected postpositional forms, and the kûl 'stress' is phrase-level emphasis/intonation (pp. 83, 100, 241).
new_statements.identity_note: Heath 2014 describes Humburi Senni (HS) of Hombori and surrounding villages, Mali = humb1243 exactly. Hacquard & Dupuis-Yakouba 1897 (in the Glottolog list for humb1243) actually describes Songhay from Timbuktu to Say (Koyra Chiini koyr1240 / Zarma zone), not Hombori, and says nothing about accent placement.

tone_statements.quote: Often these elements induce raising of the tone of the verb’s initial syllable (or mora, for monosyllabic stems) from L[ow] to H[igh]. ... Here the tone-raising is phonologically automatic, since rising-toned syllables are not allowed in HS. ... Downstep occurs when a final <HL>-toned syllable has its L-tone delinked and realized as pitch lowering on a following H-tone, as in cíjín ꜜkûl ‘every night’ from cíjîn kûl. Downstep is extremely common in HS because of the huge number of words and particles that end with a <HL>- toned syllable
tone_statements.summary: Dictionary intro: H vs L tones, <HL> falling syllables, rising syllables disallowed; downstep, upstep, floating H (+H elements) described; no tone count stated; lexicon fully tone-marked.
